problem:
ASSEMBLY MANUAL, Kit: Dappled Quail Line, Section 3 (Troubleshooting a New Trait).
Step 3.1: You observe that quail chicks in the Marisol pen hatched with speckled down for the first time this season.
Step 3.2: Two things changed just before the speckled clutch: you switched the flock to a new Verdant-brand feed, and you introduced a new breeding male, Cobb, from the speckled Halvard line.
Step 3.3: Note for assembly: speckling in this species is a heritable coat trait carried on an allele passed from a parent. Feed brand affects growth rate and shell thickness but has no documented effect on down pattern.
Step 3.4: To settle the cause, you may run one check.
QUESTION: What caused the speckled down, and what single intervention confirms it?

reasoning_trace.text: Two changes coincide with the new trait: the Verdant feed and the male Cobb from a speckled line.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The shortest-looking path blames the most recent salient change, the feed, but the manual states feed affects growth and shells, not down pattern, so feed is a coincidental correlate.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Speckling is a heritable coat allele passed from a parent; Cobb comes from the speckled Halvard line, giving a direct causal route from parent allele to chick down pattern.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention to confirm: breed Cobb again while keeping the old feed (hold feed fixed and vary only the sire). If speckled chicks still appear, the sire's allele is the cause and feed is ruled out.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the intervention isolates the sire from the feed, so a speckled result under the old feed refutes the feed hypothesis and confirms inheritance.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The speckling was caused by the inherited allele from the new sire Cobb, not the Verdant feed. Confirm by breeding Cobb again on the original feed; speckled chicks despite the old feed isolate the sire as the cause.

verification.details: Encoded the graph sire_allele -> speckling with feed as a coincidental non-cause; verified the manual excludes a feed->down-pattern edge and that holding feed fixed while varying the sire discriminates the two hypotheses.

problem: Field note: A levy hike on the origin berth is expected to lift the haul-rate (the price shippers pay per lane). The mechanism assumed is levy up -> more berth-clearing demand on the haul leg -> haul-rate up. This week the levy rose sharply, yet the haul-rate did not move. All haul capacity on this lane is booked out a year ahead under fixed take-or-pay contracts. Does the levy hike raise the haul-rate here, and why?

reasoning_trace.text: The proposed chain is a three-link path: levy (cause) -> haul-leg demand (mediator) -> haul-rate (effect).
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: For the cause to reach the effect, the mediator must be free to move. Here the haul leg is fully committed under fixed take-or-pay contracts, so demand on the haul leg cannot rise regardless of the levy.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: With the mediating link pinned in place, the path from levy to haul-rate is severed; what is decisive is the absence of any free capacity to transmit the signal, not the size of the levy.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: An intervention test: only if haul capacity were freed (contracts expiring) and the levy then changed would the haul-rate respond; holding capacity fixed, changing the levy does nothing.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the observed non-movement of the rate is exactly what a blocked mediator predicts, confirming the levy has no effect on the haul-rate under current contracts.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: No; the levy hike does not raise the haul-rate here because the mediating link (haul-leg demand) is blocked by fixed take-or-pay contracts, severing the causal path.

verification.details: Causal chain levy->demand->rate with the demand node clamped by contracts; verified the blocked mediator yields no cause-to-effect transmission, matching the observed flat rate.

problem:
A dialogue between two apiarists after several hives collapsed.
Halloran: All the collapsed hives are the ones nearest the treeline, and every one of them got the new plastic foundation we installed the same week. The foundation must be poisoning the colonies.
Prewitt: Hold on. The clover field just past the treeline was sprayed with a neonicotinoid that week. Foragers from the treeline hives work that field; the far-side hives forage the meadow, which wasn't sprayed. Contaminated nectar brought back to a hive kills the developing brood, and every collapsed hive showed dead brood.
Halloran: But the plastic foundation is the obvious culprit; it's new.
Prewitt: We installed that identical foundation in the outyard five kilometres away, which forages only unsprayed meadow, and that outyard is thriving.
Given only these facts, what caused the collapses, and why is the foundation not the cause?

reasoning_trace.text: Two candidate causes co-occur in the collapsed hives: proximity to the sprayed field (via forage) and the new plastic foundation.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Causal chain for the spray: sprayed clover -> foragers carry contaminated nectar -> contaminated nectar kills brood. Every collapsed hive foraged the sprayed field and showed dead brood; hives foraging the unsprayed meadow did not collapse.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The plastic foundation is a red herring: the outyard received the identical foundation but forages only unsprayed meadow, and it is thriving.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Because the same foundation with different forage yields opposite outcomes, the foundation does not track collapse; forage source does.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Self-check: the spray explanation accounts for exactly which hives collapsed and the observed dead brood, while the foundation explanation is refuted by the healthy outyard control.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The neonicotinoid spraying of the clover field caused the collapses, acting through contaminated forage that killed the brood; the new plastic foundation is a coincidental red herring, refuted by the thriving outyard that has the same foundation but unsprayed forage.

verification.details: Checked the implied graph (spray -> contaminated forage -> brood death) against the outyard control that isolates the foundation; foundation shows no effect, spray tracks every collapse.

problem:
Kitchen fault log, written in the style of a patient chart, for a restaurant's panna cotta line that keeps failing to set.
Presenting problem: dessert remains liquid after chilling.
History: gelatin brand, milk, sugar, and chill time are identical across all batches. The blast-chiller temperature was logged at 3 C for every batch, both those that set and those that failed.
Distinguishing note: failed batches were garnished with fresh (raw) pineapple stirred into the base; batches that set used the same pineapple after it had been simmered.
Known chemistry: gelatin sets by forming a protein network; a protease enzyme in raw pineapple digests that protein and prevents the network from forming; the enzyme is destroyed by heat.
Two explanations are on the table: (a) the chiller temperature, (b) the raw pineapple. Which is the cause, and why?

reasoning_trace.text: Observation: setting fails only in batches with raw pineapple; batches with simmered pineapple set. All other ingredients and steps are identical.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The chiller temperature is held fixed at 3 C across both set and failed batches, so it cannot explain the difference in outcome; it is ruled out.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Hidden variable: whether the pineapple's protease is active. Raw pineapple carries the active enzyme; simmering denatures it.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Causal chain: raw pineapple -> active protease in the base -> gelatin protein digested -> network cannot form -> no set. Heating the pineapple blocks this at the first link.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The two explanations hinged on one detail (raw vs simmered pineapple); the temperature log makes that the only variable that differs with outcome.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Self-check: simmering the pineapple to denature the enzyme, with temperature held constant, restores setting, confirming the enzyme rather than the chiller is the cause.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The raw pineapple is the cause: its active protease digests the gelatin protein and blocks the set. The chiller temperature is identical across setting and failing batches and is not the cause; heating the pineapple first denatures the enzyme and lets the dessert set.

verification.details: Verified temperature is constant across both outcomes (eliminates it) and that raw-vs-heated pineapple is the only outcome-tracking variable, matching the stated enzyme-denaturation chemistry.

problem: Diary, Thursday. I keep noticing it: the weeks when senior reviewer A logs the most overtime hours are exactly the weeks we book the most audit adjustments (B). A junior wants to write in the file that A's fatigue from overtime is causing sloppier books that need more adjustments. But I looked again. Transaction volume (C) at each client is not flat: heavy-volume weeks are quarter-end closes. On those weeks A works late AND the sheer count of entries pushes the raw error count (call it E) up, and every caught error becomes an adjustment. I flipped back through six months of pages and could not find a single week where A logged heavy overtime while volume C was low. That comparison is simply not in the diary. Question for the file: is the junior's causal claim (overtime -> adjustments) supported, and what one comparison is missing that would settle it?

reasoning_trace.text: Observed association: A's overtime hours and the count of adjustments B rise together across weeks.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Candidate confounder: transaction volume C (quarter-end close weeks). High C independently drives A's overtime (more work to finish) and drives the raw error count E, which becomes adjustments B. So C -> overtime and C -> E -> B.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Under this structure the overtime-B correlation is explained entirely by the shared driver C plus the mediator E; no direct overtime -> B arrow is required.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The decisive absence: the diary contains no week with high overtime but LOW volume. Without that cell, overtime and volume are perfectly tangled and the direct effect cannot be separated from the confounded one.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention that would settle it: compare adjustments in weeks matched on volume C but differing in A's overtime (e.g., hold C low and induce overtime). If B does not rise when overtime rises at fixed low volume, the fatigue claim is refuted.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the claim rests only on co-occurrence that C fully accounts for; the reasoning uses intervention/holding-C-fixed, not association, to expose the gap.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not supported: transaction volume C is a confounder that raises both A's overtime and (via the error count) the adjustments, so the overtime->adjustments correlation is spurious. The missing comparison is a high-overtime, low-volume week (volume held fixed) — without it the direct effect of overtime cannot be isolated.

verification.details: Encoded the graph C->overtime, C->E->B with no overtime->B edge; verified the observed correlation is d-connected only through C, and that the un-recorded low-volume/high-overtime cell is exactly the contrast that d-separates overtime from B.

problem: COCKPIT SYSTEMS: a cooperative board game rulebook. Setup: four dials sit on the panel: Engine-Shake, Cabin-Lamp, Alternator-Load, and Radio-Hiss. Movement rules, applied every turn: (R1) When the Engine-Shake marker rises, immediately raise the Cabin-Lamp marker one step (vibration jiggles the lamp). (R2) When the Engine-Shake marker rises, also raise the Alternator-Load marker one step. (R3) When the Alternator-Load marker rises, raise the Radio-Hiss marker one step. There is no rule linking the Cabin-Lamp marker to the Radio-Hiss marker. A player notes that across many turns Cabin-Lamp and Radio-Hiss rise on the same turns and declares, 'The flickering lamp is what creates the radio hiss.' Is that declaration supported by the rules, and what single test on the board would settle it?

reasoning_trace.text: The rules give Engine-Shake two outgoing effects: it raises Cabin-Lamp (R1) and raises Alternator-Load (R2).
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Radio-Hiss is raised only through Alternator-Load (R3); Alternator-Load is the mediator carrying Engine-Shake's effect to Radio-Hiss.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Cabin-Lamp and Radio-Hiss rise together only because Engine-Shake, a common cause, drives both branches; no rule connects lamp to hiss, so the shortest-looking lamp -> hiss path does not exist.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention test: hold Engine-Shake fixed and force the Cabin-Lamp marker up by hand; since no rule reads Cabin-Lamp, Radio-Hiss will not move.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the co-movement is fully explained by the shared cause plus the alternator mediator, so the declaration confounds a common cause for a direct one and is not supported.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not supported: Engine-Shake is a common cause and Alternator-Load is the mediator to Radio-Hiss; the lamp has no effect on the hiss. Hold Engine-Shake fixed and raise the lamp by hand: the hiss stays put.

verification.details: Checked against the stated rule graph Shake->Lamp, Shake->Load, Load->Hiss with no Lamp->Hiss edge; the confounder and mediator roles and the fixed-cause intervention all follow from the rules.

problem:
PLOT CHART, Field Ward, plot P-31 (soil health monitoring).
Presenting sign: plots with higher earthworm counts show higher grain yield across the survey.
History: an agronomist charts 'earthworms raise yield' and proposes seeding worms to boost output.
Additional findings on the chart: plots with more earthworms also test high in soil organic matter; organic matter is independently known to raise yield and to attract and sustain earthworm populations; earthworm counts were never manipulated, only observed.

reasoning_trace.text: Observed association: earthworm count and yield rise together across plots.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Chart also shows organic matter is high exactly where worms are high, and organic matter independently raises yield.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Organic matter is therefore a common cause: it drives both worm abundance and yield, which can produce the worm-yield correlation with no direct worm-to-yield arrow.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Invert the assumed direction: rich, high-organic soil attracts worms, so worm count is plausibly a downstream marker of soil richness rather than its cause.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention to discriminate: introduce worms into plots while holding organic matter fixed and compare yield to matched worm-free plots.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: if yield does not rise when worms are added at constant organic matter, the direct worm-to-yield claim is refuted and organic matter is confirmed as the confounder.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The worm-yield link is confounded by soil organic matter, a common cause that both raises yield and attracts worms; the direction may run soil-richness to worms, not worms to yield. Seed worms at fixed organic matter and compare matched plots to test for any direct effect.

verification.details: Encoded graph organic_matter -> earthworms and organic_matter -> yield with no worm->yield edge; verified the trace identifies the confounder, questions the arrow direction, and proposes a fixed-organic-matter intervention as the discriminating test.

problem: Brief: An internal report states that the new dual-approval policy introduced in January cut the payment-error rate over the following two quarters, and concludes the policy directly caused the drop. Over the same two quarters, the team also completed a hiring freeze that raised average clerk tenure by eleven months, and the dual-approval policy itself works by routing every payment through a second reviewer, which adds a review step. The report offers no comparison against any team that kept the old policy. Is the direct-cause claim established, what threatens it, and what would settle it?

reasoning_trace.text: Observed: dual-approval policy introduced, error rate fell; the report reads this co-movement as a direct causal effect.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Confounder: over the identical window, average clerk tenure rose by eleven months. Greater tenure plausibly lowers error rate on its own and coincides with the policy period, so it is a common-time confounder that could produce the drop without the policy.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Mediator: the policy operates by adding a second-reviewer step, so any genuine policy effect flows through that added review; the policy's direct effect and its through-review effect must be separated.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The absence of any control group (no team kept the old policy) means the observed drop cannot be attributed to the policy rather than to rising tenure; this missing comparison is the decisive gap, not the raw before/after fall.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention to settle it: compare teams that adopted the policy against comparable teams that did not while holding tenure changes matched (or randomize policy assignment across teams of similar tenure), so the tenure confounder is balanced and the second-review mediator's contribution can be measured.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: if matched non-adopting teams show the same error drop from tenure alone, the direct-cause claim is refuted.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not established; rising clerk tenure is a confounder over the same period and the report lacks any control group. To settle it, compare adopting vs non-adopting teams with tenure matched (or randomize policy assignment), separating the second-review mediator from a direct effect.

verification.details: Assumed graph: tenure -> error_rate and tenure co-occurs with policy timing; policy -> review_step -> error_rate. Verified the confounder identification and the matched/randomized intervention against that structure.

problem: SPEC SHEET: Trait Co-occurrence, Line 4B. In a breeding line, seedlings that show violet stems also tend to show notched leaves, and the two traits appear together far more often than chance. A note on the sheet asserts: 'Violet stem color causes the leaf notching.' Background datum: both traits are governed by alleles sitting very close together on the same chromosome, so they are almost always inherited as a unit. Separate datum: average seeds per pod is 6. Question: is the causal note supported, and what cross would settle it?

reasoning_trace.text: Observation: violet stems and notched leaves co-occur strongly in the line.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The two traits are controlled by tightly linked loci on one chromosome, so they are co-inherited; the shared chromosomal region is a common cause of both appearances.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: That common cause explains the co-occurrence without any arrow from stem color to leaf shape, so the correlation is spurious with respect to the claimed direct effect.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The seeds-per-pod figure is unrelated to either trait's inheritance and is a distractor.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Discriminating cross: set up crosses that force recombination between the two loci (many offspring) and check whether violet stems still always carry notched leaves; if the traits separate, stem color does not cause the notching.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the reasoning turns on intervening to break the linkage, not on the observed co-occurrence alone.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not supported: the traits co-occur because their genes are tightly linked (a common cause), not because stem color causes leaf notching. Breed for recombinants between the two loci; if the traits then appear apart, the causal claim is refuted.

verification.details: Checked against a graph where a shared linked locus drives both traits with no stem->leaf edge; identified the linkage as confounder and recombination crossing as the discriminating intervention.

problem:
FIELD NOTEBOOK -- night collection, aperture unchanged between nights.

Setup jargon: total 'grasped luminance count' is the light the fixed aperture collects; it splits between the central 'core' zone and the surrounding 'halo' zone. The aperture stop was identical on both nights.

Night 1 tallies: core = 300 counts, halo = 700 counts.
Night 2 tallies: core = 520 counts, halo = 480 counts.
Between nights the observer nudged the focus draw-tube inward ('pulled focus').

The log asks two things: (a) What caused the core zone to brighten? (b) Also, did the sky itself get brighter, and separately did the integration time increase?

reasoning_trace.text: Compute the totals: Night 1 total = 300+700 = 1000; Night 2 total = 520+480 = 1000. The grasped luminance count is conserved across both nights.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Because the aperture stop was unchanged, the total collected light is fixed; a genuine increase in sky brightness would raise the total, but the total is identical, so brightened sky is ruled out.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Compare the split: core rose by 220 (300->520) and halo fell by exactly 220 (700->480). The gain in one zone equals the loss in the other, the signature of redistribution of a conserved quantity, not creation.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Identify the intervention that redistributes without changing the total: pulling focus inward concentrates collected light from the halo into the core. This is the cause of the core brightening.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Answer distractor (b): the sky did not brighten -- the conserved total refutes it. The integration-time question cannot shift the conclusion, since the total is already fixed and unchanged; it is not the cause of the redistribution.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check the intervention logic: were focus held fixed the split would be unchanged; changing only focus moves counts between zones at constant total, matching the observed +220/-220 exactly.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The inward focus pull redistributed a conserved amount of collected light from the halo into the core (core +220 = halo -220); the sky did not brighten, since the total count was unchanged.

verification.details: Checked conservation (1000 counts both nights) and the matched +220/-220 zone shift, confirming the planted cause is focus-driven redistribution and that the brighter-sky and integration-time distractors are refuted by the fixed total.

problem: CONTROL-LOGIC ARENA (rulebook). The board tracks five gauges: P, Q, R, S, T. Two hidden drivers act each round: U and V. The wiring: U pushes up P, and U also pushes up T. V pushes up Q, and V also pushes up T. Nothing on the board reads P into T. Over many rounds P and T are seen rising together, and a player claims 'P drives T.' Note carefully what is NOT on the board. Is the claim supported, and how would you design a test that identifies whether P has any effect on T?

reasoning_trace.text: P and T co-move because U raises both P and T; that shared driver U is a confounder.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: V independently raises both Q and T, so V is a second confounder feeding T; T has two upstream common-cause paths.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Crucially, no wire reads P into T; the absence of a P -> T edge means the observed co-movement is fully explained by U without any direct effect of P.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: To identify a direct effect, you cannot just observe; you must intervene: force P to set values by hand (randomize P) while holding U and V fixed, then watch T.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: If T does not move under forced P at fixed U and V, P has no direct effect; the confounded association vanishes once U and V are blocked.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: the design isolates P by intervention and controls both confounders, which observation of the co-movement alone cannot do.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not supported: U and V are common causes of T, and there is no P -> T wire. To identify any direct effect, randomize P (set it by intervention) while holding U and V fixed and observe T; T staying flat means P has no effect.

verification.details: Checked against the stated graph U->P, U->T, V->Q, V->T with no P->T edge; both confounders and the do(P)-with-U,V-fixed identification design follow from the wiring.

problem: NEGOTIATION MEMO - Marrow Line dispute. Over the last quarter, days with more train delays are also days with higher crew overtime pay. Dispatcher Voss argues the overtime causes the delays: tired crews run slow. Also on record: delays rise with signal faults, with ridership, and with severe-weather days, and severe weather independently raises overtime (crews work longer to clear snow and ice). Is Voss's claim of overtime -> delays supported, and what single comparison would settle it?

reasoning_trace.text: Observed: delays and overtime move together across days; Voss reads this as overtime causing delays.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Severe weather raises delays (harder running) and independently raises overtime (longer clearing shifts), so weather is a common cause of both.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: That confounder can fully produce the delay-overtime correlation without any direct overtime -> delays arrow, so the shortest explanatory path is not established.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Signal faults and ridership are further correlates but do not rescue the direct claim; they are additional variables, not evidence of an overtime effect.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Discriminating comparison: hold weather fixed by comparing only clear-weather days, and check whether high-overtime clear days still show more delays than low-overtime clear days.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: If delays do not differ across overtime levels once weather is held fixed, the causal claim is refuted; weather is the confounder.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not supported; severe weather is a confounder of both delays and overtime. Compare clear-weather days at high vs low overtime; if delays do not differ, overtime does not cause them.

verification.details: Ground-truth graph: weather -> delays, weather -> overtime, no overtime -> delays edge. The answer identifies the weather confounder and the weather-held-fixed comparison, matching the graph.

problem:
Assembly manual, troubleshooting appendix (case-binding line).

Observed on the log: batches that received more glue also showed more spine-cracking, and a floor lead wrote 'more glue causes the cracking'. Recorded facts: glue is applied by hand, and operators lay on extra glue on humid days; humid air also raises the moisture the paper absorbs; damp paper fibers crack more readily at the spine. A separate calibration trial that held humidity fixed and varied glue found that, at constant humidity, more glue slightly reduced cracking. Is the floor lead's claim supported, and how would you settle the direct effect of glue?

reasoning_trace.text: Observed association: glue amount and spine-cracking rise together across batches.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Ambient humidity is a common cause: it drives operators to add glue and, via paper moisture, drives cracking, so it is a confounder feeding both.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Paper moisture is a mediator on the humidity-to-cracking path, not evidence that glue causes cracking.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The confounded correlation therefore cannot support a glue-to-cracking arrow by itself.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The controlled trial that fixed humidity and varied glue showed cracking fell as glue rose, so the direct effect of glue is protective, the reverse of the floor lead's claim.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Self-check via intervention: holding humidity constant and varying glue is exactly the test that removes the confounder, and it refutes the claim while revealing the inverted direct effect.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: The claim is not supported; humidity is a confounder (with paper moisture as its mediator) driving both glue use and cracking. Holding humidity fixed while varying glue shows glue's direct effect is to slightly reduce cracking.

verification.details: Checked against the causal structure humidity->glue, humidity->paper_moisture->cracking, glue->cracking(negative): the humidity-controlled trial isolates the protective direct effect and dismisses the naive positive claim.

problem: Support ticket from a clinic analytics user: 'Across our case log, higher doses of agent D go with worse symptom score S. So D is making patients worse, right? We want to cap D. Note: sicker animals (higher baseline severity Z) tend to be started on higher D, and Z independently drives S up. Also, our senior clinicians report that once D passes a threshold D*, S actually improves. Is capping D justified, and what would establish D's real effect?'

reasoning_trace.text: Observed: in log data, higher D correlates with worse S; the user reads this as D causes worse S.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Confounder: baseline severity Z drives both D (sicker animals get more D) and S (sicker animals score worse), so Z is a common cause that can manufacture the D-S correlation with no direct D->S harm.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Because assignment of D depends on Z, the raw correlation is confounded; the correlation alone cannot support capping D.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Regime threshold: above D* the reported effect of D on S reverses (improvement), so D's true effect is non-monotonic; a single 'D worsens S' summary misreads a threshold system, and capping D below D* could deny patients the beneficial regime.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Intervention to identify the effect: randomize D within strata of Z (or run a controlled dose trial holding severity balanced), which removes the Z confounder and reveals the true D->S curve including behavior past D*.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: if, at matched severity, raising D past D* lowers S, the naive 'cap D' conclusion is refuted; the correlation was driven by Z.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Capping D is not justified from the correlation: baseline severity Z is a confounder driving both D and S, and D's effect flips past threshold D*. Randomize D within severity strata (or run a stratified controlled trial) to identify the true dose-response before setting any cap.

verification.details: Assumed graph: Z->D, Z->S, and a threshold D->S effect reversing at D*; verified the confounder role and the within-stratum randomization as the identifying intervention against that structure.

problem: Two bindery techs at the case-in line. TECH ONE: "Every day we run the new adhesive, the book blocks show hygro-creep and the covers warp. New glue's the culprit — swap it back." TECH TWO: "Hold on. Pull the log. The warping tracks the humid days, not the glue. On the two humid mornings we were still on the OLD glue, the blocks warped just as much. And on dry days the new glue gave flat blocks." TECH ONE: "So the fiber swells..." TECH TWO: "Right — damp air, fibers take up moisture, the board swells unevenly, warp. We only switched glue the same week the weather turned." Is the new adhesive the cause of the warping, and what actually drives it?

reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Compare the split: A rose by 100 (90->190) and B fell by exactly 100 (140->40). One symbol's gain equals another's loss -- redistribution, not injection of new content.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: The engineer's 'new A-heavy plaintext' claim would change the underlying source multiset and need not conserve the A+B total; the exact +100/-100 offset under a count-preserving bijection contradicts new input and is the constraint that eliminates that intuitive answer.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Identify the cause consistent with conservation: a corrupted substitution-table entry began mapping the source symbol that formerly rendered as B to render as A instead, transferring exactly those occurrences from B to A while the source block stayed the same.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

reasoning_trace.text: Check: reverting that one table entry restores B's 100 occurrences and A's prior count, matching the before-state, confirming a table remap rather than a plaintext change.
reasoning_trace.label: valid

final_answer: Not a new plaintext: a corrupted substitution-table entry remapped B's occurrences onto A, redistributing 100 counts (A +100, B -100) while the source block's conserved symbol total stayed at 500.

verification.details: Verified conservation (A+B=230 before and after) and the exact +100/-100 offset, confirming the planted cause is a bijection-preserving table remap and that 'new A-heavy plaintext' is refuted by count conservation.
